1. While SELENOP ensures the selenium transport from the liver to other organs, high GPX1 levels within the liver might serve
as an indirect selenium storage which can be immediately released upon limited selenium supply.

Selenium
415


Selenoprotein synthesis is regulated by the selenium supply and there is a hierarchy of expression of individual selenoproteins
and of retention of selenium in different organs and tissues. The organ-speciﬁc hierarchy under selenium deﬁciency mostly depends
on the APOER2-mediated uptake of SELENOP from the blood maintaining e.g., brain selenium levels at the expense of other
organs. Selenium crosses the placenta readily, and breast milk selenium concentration is responsive to changes in maternal sele-
nium intake. The liver is supposed to react most sensitive toward a limited selenium supply with a drop of selenoprotein expression,
especially GPX1. Nonspeciﬁc incorporation of selenomethionine into proteins contributes to tissue selenium levels but is not
immediately available for synthesis of selenoproteins until protein is catabolized. Selenium levels in tissues are inﬂuenced by die-
tary intake, as reﬂected in the wide variation in blood selenium concentrations of residents of countries with differing soil selenium
levels (Hong and Diamond, 2020; Roman et al., 2014).
